entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.work: "The Barrier of Meaning," Letters in Mathematical Physics 10 (1985), pp. 97-99; opening address at the conference "Evolution, Games and Learning," Los Alamos National Laboratory, 20-25 May 1985; reprinted in Indiscrete Thoughts
entries.caution: Read from the transcription on disk, whose header records the venue and printing. Rota’s address was given at Los Alamos in May 1985, the year after Ulam’s death.
entries.quote: I then saw the man in his true light. The man who had the highest record of accurate guesses in mathematics, the man who could beat engineers at their game, who could size up characters and events in a flash, was a member of an all-but-extinct profession, the profession of the prophet.

entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.work: "The Barrier of Meaning," Letters in Mathematical Physics 10 (1985), pp. 97-99; opening address at the conference "Evolution, Games and Learning," Los Alamos National Laboratory, 20-25 May 1985; reprinted in Indiscrete Thoughts
entries.caution: Read from the transcription on disk, whose header records the venue and printing. Rota’s address was given at Los Alamos in May 1985, the year after Ulam’s death.
entries.quote: He shared with the men of the Old Testament and with the Oracle at Delphi the heavy burden of instant vision. And like all professional prophets, he suffered from a condition that Sigmund Freud would have labeled “a Proteus complex.” It is unfortunate that Freud did not count any prophets among his patients.

entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.work: quoted in Gian-Carlo Rota, “The Barrier of Meaning,” Letters in Mathematical Physics 10 (1985), pp. 97-99
entries.context: Rota’s framing: he had asked Ulam why he constantly wanted company, “and his answer gave him away.”
entries.caution: Read from the transcription on disk, whose header records the venue and printing. Rota’s address was given at Los Alamos in May 1985, the year after Ulam’s death.
entries.quote: When I am alone, I am forced to think things out, and I see so much that I would rather not think about!

entries.quote: In bygone days, the Sybil’s dark mumblings would be interpreted by trained specialists, Hermeneuts they were called, who were charged with the task of expressing her cryptic messages in lapidary Greek sentences. In Ulam’s case, the Los Alamos Laboratory would instead hire consultants, charged with the task of expressing his cryptic messages in the dilapidated jargon of modern mathematics.

entries.quote: Luckily, some of Stan Ulam’s pronouncements were tape-recorded by Francoise Ulam. When they are edited and published, the younger generations will find, if they are still willing to read, that some ideas they believe to be their own had been anticipated in his flashes of foresight.

entries.speaker: John von Neumann
entries.work: Letter to Erwin Schrödinger, in John von Neumann: Selected Letters, ed. Miklós Rédei, History of Mathematics vol. 27 (AMS/LMS, 2005)
entries.locus: pp. 211-213; quoted in Rédei’s introductory commentary §5.3
entries.context: Rédei’s framing: “Von Neumann’s position is that the presence of correlations between spatially separated quantum systems is not, in and by itself, reason for concern.”
entries.caution: Read from Rédei’s introductory commentary on disk, section 5.3, which quotes the letter and gives the date. The letter itself is printed at pp. 211-213 of the volume.
entries.quote: I cannot accept your section 4. completely. I think that the difficulties you hint at are “pseudo-problems”. The “action at distance” in the case under consideration says only that even if there is no dynamical interaction between two systems (e.g. because they are far removed from each other), the systems can display statistical correlations. This is not at all specific for quantum mechanics, it happens classically as well.

entries.speaker: John von Neumann
entries.work: Letter to Erwin Schrödinger, in John von Neumann: Selected Letters, ed. Miklós Rédei, History of Mathematics vol. 27 (AMS/LMS, 2005)
entries.locus: pp. 211-213; quoted in Rédei’s introductory commentary §5.4
entries.caution: Read from Rédei’s introductory commentary on disk, section 5.3, which quotes the letter and gives the date. The letter itself is printed at pp. 211-213 of the volume.
entries.quote: And of course quantum electrodynamics proves that quantum mechanics and the special theory of relativity are compatible “philosophically” -- quantum electrodynamic fails only because of the concrete form of Maxwell’s equations in the vicinity of a charge.

entries.speaker: Miklós Rédei
entries.work: Introductory commentary to John von Neumann: Selected Letters, ed. Miklós Rédei, History of Mathematics vol. 27 (AMS/LMS, 2005)
entries.caution: Rédei is the volume’s editor; this is his own commentary, not von Neumann’s words.
entries.quote: There is, however, no record of any exchange between von Neumann and Einstein on this subject, nor did von Neumann ever express any views on the EPR paper’s argument -- the only exception I am aware of being von Neumann’s letter to Schrodinger published in the present volume (April 11, 1936).

entries.speaker: John von Neumann
entries.work: Letter to P. A. M. Dirac, in John von Neumann: Selected Letters, ed. Miklós Rédei, History of Mathematics vol. 27 (AMS/LMS, 2005)
entries.context: Rédei’s framing: to avoid the divergence arising from point-likeness of charges, von Neumann tried to quantize space.
entries.caution: Read from Rédei’s introductory commentary on disk, section 5.3, which quotes the letter and gives the date. The letter itself is printed at pp. 211-213 of the volume.
entries.quote: It should be perhaps desirable, to have operators X, Y, Z which have discrete (point) spectra, in order to avoid the difficulties connected with the point electron (in electrodynamics).

entries.speaker: Martin Gardner
entries.work: Preface to Stanislaw Ulam, Science, Computers, and People: From the Tree of Mathematics (Birkhäuser, 1986)
entries.context: The full list Gardner gives is “Cellular automata theory, which he proposed to von Neumann; the Monte Carlo method of solving intractable problems, not only in probability theory but in areas such as number theory where the method would not have been thought applicable; and his work on nonlinear processes that anticipated today’s interest in solitons and ‘chaos.’”
entries.caution: Gardner’s preface, not Ulam’s or von Neumann’s words. Read from the transcription on disk; the “Preface by Martin Gardner” heading is at line 42 of that file. The text this was read from is not reproduced in this collection; the work is cited to its published edition in URLS.md.
entries.quote: To mention only three: Cellular automata theory, which he proposed to von Neumann; the Monte Carlo method of solving intractable problems, not only in probability theory but in areas such as number theory where the method would not have been thought applicable; and his work on nonlinear processes that anticipated today’s interest in solitons and “chaos.”

entries.speaker: Martin Gardner
entries.work: Preface to Stanislaw Ulam, Science, Computers, and People: From the Tree of Mathematics (Birkhäuser, 1986)

entries.quote: We still do not know—it remains a government secret—what jumped into Ulam’s head that made it possible for Edward Teller to build an H-bomb.
